text:
The three days of travel may be read as a kind of suspended sentence, in which nothing outward happens and yet everything of consequence is done. The narrator dwells upon the servants, the wood, the knife, and the fire; by dwelling on them he names the instruments of the act before the act itself. Obedience and horror go together through the whole journey, and neither is suffered to prevail. Faith, in this story, is an ordered relation of persons and acts, with little of the character of a feeling.

Compared with the earlier promise, the scene stands nearer to it than at first appears. The reader is reminded that Isaac is the child of the covenant, through whom the nations are to be blessed; and that promise is here made a test. All rests upon one word, _hineni_, "here I am," which Abraham speaks three times: to God, to Isaac, to the angel. Each time it means something different, and costs him more; in Abraham's mouth the language of presence is the language of loss.
